card.hook: Caernarfon Castle is so big and so solid that your phone will happily fill the whole screen with nothing but stone and sky. That's a good problem to have.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon near Tan y Bont, about 20 m north-east of the subject. Face south-west and the castle is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the full length of the walls and towers in. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and if your phone has 2x or 5x, use it to pick out a tower top or the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line up a wall or tower edge with an up-and-down line so the castle doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, lower light that shows off the texture of the stone. Midday sun can be harsh, and it's often busier too.
card.selfie_here: Try Y Maes (Castle Square), the open square right in front of the castle. Use your front camera, turn your back to the castle, and hold the phone a bit lower so the walls rise up behind your shoulder. We haven't confirmed this spot with a selfie, so check the angle as you go.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Pont yr Aber footbridge, across the River Seiont at the bottom of Castle Hill, to frame the full south front of the castle, ideally with moored boats in the foreground.
card.rules_and_safety: Drones aren't allowed, so leave yours at home. Going inside may be ticketed, so check the official Cadw site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole castle, then one close-up of a single tower, and see if friends can match the two.
card.good_to_know: King Edward I began the stone castle in 1283, on a spot where a Norman motte-and-bailey castle had stood since the late 11th century. It was meant to be the administrative centre of north Wales, which is why it's so big. It hosted the investiture of the Prince of Wales in 1911 and 1969, and it's part of a World Heritage Site.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon near Tan y Bont, about 20 m north-east of the subject. Face south-west and the castle is right in front of you.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot was found. No page describes a spot where a visitor stands with the castle directly behind them, so the Castle Square entry is an inference from the square lying in front of the castle, and it should be checked on the ground. Both the Wales Coast Path page (about five years old) and the Tripadvisor thread (about fourteen years old) are dated, so the footbridge and access details may have changed. Pages say that drones are not allowed and that photography is generally allowed inside the castle, but none mention selfie sticks or tripods, so no rule on those is reported. Several sources say to cross the bridge over the River Seiont for the best view; they say nothing about a safety hazard, so the safety field is left blank.

card.hook: This is your 'I was here' shot, and it only takes a minute. Get one tidy picture of the museum for your records, then spend your time inside.
card.stand_here: Stand near Allt y Castell, about 35 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The museum is right in front of you and you can fit all of it in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole frontage. If you can't step back far enough, try 0.5x, but keep the phone level and people away from the edges, where they can look stretched. Then move closer or go to 2x or more (depending on your phone) for a detail you can see on the building.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the walls with them so the building stands straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in your shot. Around midday on a bright day, expect harder shadows on the walls.
card.selfie_here: Walk to Pont yr Aber (the Aber Swing Bridge) over the River Seiont. Stand on the footbridge facing away from the castle so it's behind you, use the front camera, and try 0.5x to squeeze in the towers. For a watery backdrop, try the quayside by the Anglesey Arms, with the Eagle Tower and banded walls behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to cross Pont yr Aber and walk the road on the far side (the Aber Foreshore Road direction), then stand you in front of the castle so they can frame the whole thing, ideally with boats in the river.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site before you go, as entry to the museum may be ticketed or restricted.
card.challenge: Take your straight-on shot with the gridlines, then find one small detail on the building that most people walk past and zoom in on it.
card.good_to_know: The Royal Welch Fusiliers Museum is the second stop on the Caernarfon map. It's a place to visit as well as photograph, so leave yourself time to see what's inside. The official site is the best place to check visiting details.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Allt y Castell, about 35 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The museum is right in front of you and you can fit all of it in.

card.hook: Here's a plot twist: the best viewpoint for Segontium doesn't really show Segontium. What you get from the top of Ben Twthill is the scene around it, with Caernarfon's rooftops, the castle, the Strait and the mountains beyond.
card.stand_here: Stand at the top of Ben Twthill. Cross the footbridge over the main road, then take the path opposite St David and St Helen's Church up the hill. Face out over the rooftops and castle towards the Menai Strait; Segontium is off to the south-east, so it's the story behind the picture rather than the star of it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the rooftops, the Strait and the mountains. Then try 1x, or 2x to 5x if your phone has them, to pick out the castle.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, with the town and castle low in the frame and the mountains as your backdrop.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon light suits this area, with Snowdonia as the backdrop. It's a good excuse to skip the midday rush.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, so you fit in with the view behind you. Keep your arm slightly raised, and let the town and hills sit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is encouraged throughout the museum and the outdoor site. Ben Twthill can be windy, so keep a firm grip on your phone. For the fort itself, check the official Cadw site first, as the gate has been found locked on at least one visit.
card.challenge: Try a slow panorama from left to right and see if you can keep the castle neatly in the middle without any wobble.
card.good_to_know: Segontium was founded by Agricola in AD 77 or 78 and built to hold about a thousand auxiliary soldiers. It was the most important Roman fort in the north of Wales. Coins found here suggest it was still in use until at least the year 394.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the top of Ben Twthill. Cross the footbridge over the main road, then take the path opposite St David and St Helen's Church up the hill. Face out over the rooftops and castle towards the Menai Strait; Segontium is off to the south-east, so it's the story behind the picture rather than the star of it.

rules.rule: Photography is encouraged throughout the museum and the outdoor site.

sources.title: Segontium Roman Fort Museum, Caernarfon - Museums in London

selfie_research.notes: No selfie spot found. None of the pages I read names a standing position where a visitor has the Segontium fort behind them, and none names a spot for a passer-by to photograph a visitor with the whole fort in view. The Ben Twthill viewpoint is described as a good photo spot over Caernarfon, but no page links it to a view of the fort, so I left it out. The museumsuk page says the fort foundations photograph well in morning or late afternoon light with Snowdonia as a backdrop, but it names no spot. Reviewers on Tripadvisor reported a locked gate and a site fenced off from the road, so check access before you go. The pages also disagree on the address: Britain Express puts the fort on the A4085 and Evendo says Constantine Road. No page mentions selfie sticks or tripods, and no page gives a safety point.

card.hook: Everyone heads for the castle, but this old wall just sits quietly nearby, looking rough, weathered and brilliant. It's a good place to slow down and take a few frames.
card.stand_here: Stand on Hole In the Wall Street, at the Castle Ditch stretch of the town wall. The spot is about 666 m (roughly 8 minutes on foot) to the south-east, so follow the wall on the map rather than guessing at side streets. Face the wall from beside the street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x if the street feels narrow, so you can fit the full height of the wall. Use 1x for a natural view, then try 2x or more (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the wall up with the horizontal lines so it looks nice and straight.
card.best_time: Go in daylight when the sun isn't directly behind the wall. An early start is likely to be quieter. The narrow street can be shaded, so check the light on the day.
card.selfie_here: Try Hole in the Wall Street, with the medieval wall on the other side of the street. It's a shady lane, so the wall can sit behind you without much clutter. Use the front camera, or 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone so the wall is over your shoulder. The stretch just north of the East Gate is another good one, as Cadw names it among the best-preserved bits of wall.
card.ask_someone: For a wider shot with the castle, cross the Seiont by the castle, walk up the river to the shore, and ask your companion to photograph you from there (the exact point is approximate).
card.rules_and_safety: Access to the wall-walk is limited, so check the official site (Cadw) before you go. The walls themselves can be seen from the street.
card.challenge: Find a doorway or window in the wall and use it to show how big the stonework is. Bonus points if a friend walks through at just the right moment.
card.good_to_know: The walls were built between 1283 and 1292 under Edward I, at the same time as the castle. The circuit is 734 m long, with eight towers and two medieval gatehouses. They were badly damaged in the 1294 revolt, repaired the next year, and the town's defences later held out against Owain Glyndŵr's attacks in 1403 and 1404.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Hole In the Wall Street, at the Castle Ditch stretch of the town wall. The spot is about 666 m (roughly 8 minutes on foot) to the south-east, so follow the wall on the map rather than guessing at side streets. Face the wall from beside the street.

card.hook: It's 75 metres of plain concrete and steel, and it makes a better photo than it has any right to. One long straight line over the river, with Caernarfon Castle hanging about nearby.
card.stand_here: Stand near Pont yr Aber, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the bridge and step back until the whole span fits in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the bridge. Switch to zoom 0.5x if you want the whole span and the surroundings in one shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and run the deck along one of them, then tap the bridge and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright so the steelwork doesn't turn into a silhouette.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people on the bridge. On a still day the river may give you a nice reflection.
card.selfie_here: Try the park bank where the bridge meets Coed Helen park, on the castle side. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the view sits over your shoulder. Check the framing on your screen before you smile, because the bridge may not squeeze in.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the castle-side end by the Watergate entrance, at the bottom of Castle Hill, while you stand at the park end so the whole bridge runs between you.
card.rules_and_safety: When the bridge opens for pleasure boats, an alarm bell sounds and the safety barriers close, so keep clear of them while it swings. It has been closed for maintenance before and may only be open to foot traffic at set times, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for someone to stroll across and catch them in the middle of the span, with the horizon dead level and the castle end looking perfectly upright.
card.good_to_know: This bridge was built in 1970, runs on electricity and is about 75 metres long. It replaced an earlier swing bridge that opened on St David's Day, 1 March 1900, which had itself replaced a ferry. That older bridge was demolished in 1969, and a bailey bridge stood in its place for a short time.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near Pont yr Aber, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the bridge and step back until the whole span fits in the frame.

card.hook: Look at the castle next door, then look at this gate. The castle's towers have lots of sides, but Porth yr Aur's two towers are round and crenelated, and that clash of shapes is your photo.
card.stand_here: Near Sowth o Ffrans, stand about 10 m west of the gate, right at the phone icon on the map. Face east and the gatehouse is straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: You're close, so start at zoom 0.5x to fit both towers and the low barbican in. Keep your phone level so the walls don't lean inwards. Then switch to zoom 1x or 2x for a tighter shot of the battlements and the cannon.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put one round tower either side of the centre line, then tap the stonework and slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright so the walls keep their colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people wandering into your frame.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Promenade just outside the gate and turn to face the water, so the gateway is behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and hold your phone a bit low so both towers fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Promenade directly opposite the gate's west front, where the barbican juts out towards them, while you pose in front of it so the whole gateway and both towers fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: The gate is home to the Royal Welsh Yacht Club, so enjoy it and photograph it from the outside.
card.challenge: Get one photo with a round gate tower and a many-sided castle tower in the same frame, then see if a friend can spot the difference.
card.good_to_know: Porth yr Aur was begun in 1283, at the same time as the castle, and finished by 1292. It was badly damaged in the Welsh revolt of 1294 and then repaired. Since 1854 it has been home to the Royal Welsh Yacht Club, and one of the Napoleonic-period cannon is still on the gate. It's part of the Castles and Town Walls of King Edward in Gwynedd UNESCO World Heritage Site.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Near Sowth o Ffrans, stand about 10 m west of the gate, right at the phone icon on the map. Face east and the gatehouse is straight ahead of you.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found gives a dedicated photo spot for Porth yr Aur, so the selfie spot and the passer-by spot are inferred from the gate's orientation to the Promenade, not taken from a photo guide. The Pont yr Aber bridge and the across-the-river views in the Wales Coast Path guide are for Caernarfon Castle, not this gate, so I left them out. No page states selfie stick or tripod rules for this site. The only Porth yr Aur 'safety' item I found is a legend about not speaking while passing through, which is folklore rather than safety, so I left it blank. The building is the Royal Welsh Yacht Club, and the Cadw listing is the most reliable source for its position. The Grokipedia entry was not used because it is an unreliable source.
